source_text: Καὶ μὴν καὶ τὴν δύναμιν, ὡς ἔστιν ἀρκοῦσα πρὸς τὴν τῶν σωμάτων ἀνάστασιν, δείκνυσιν ἡ τούτων αὐτῶν γένεσις. Εἰ γὰρ μὴ ὄντα κατὰ τὴν πρώτην σύστασιν ἐποίησε τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων σώματα καὶ τὰς τούτων ἀρχάς, καὶ διαλυθέντα, καθ᾿ ὃν ἂν τύχῃ τρόπον, ἀναστήσει μετὰ τῆς ἴσης εὐμαρείας· ἐπ᾿ ἴσης γὰρ αὐτῷ καὶ τοῦτο δυνατόν. Καὶ τῷ λόγῳ βλάβος οὐδέν, κἂν ἐξ ὕλης ὑποθῶνταί τινες τὰς πρώτας ἀρχάς, κἂν ἐκ τῶν στοιχείων ὡς πρώτων τὰ σώματα τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, κἂν ἐκ σπερμάτων. Ἧς γάρ ἐστι δυνάμεως καὶ τὴν παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς νενομισμένην ἄμορφον οὖσαν μορφῶσαι, καὶ τὴν ἀνείδεον καὶ ἀδιακόσμητον πολλοῖς καὶ διαφόροις εἴδεσι κοσμῆσαι, καὶ τὰ μέρη τῶν στοιχείων εἰς ἓν συναγαγεῖν, καὶ τὸ σπέρμα ἓν ὂν καὶ ἁπλοῦν εἰς πολλὰ διελεῖν, καὶ τὸ ἀδιάρθρωτον διαρθρῶσαι, καὶ τῷ μὴ ζῶντι δοῦναι ζωήν, τῆς αὐτῆς ἐστι καὶ τὸ διαλελυμένον ἑνῶσαι, καὶ τὸ κείμενον ἀναστῆσαι, καὶ τὸ τεθνηκὸς ζωοποιῆσαι πάλιν, καὶ τὸ φθαρτὸν μεταβαλεῖν εἰς ἀρθαρσίαν. Τοῦ αὐτοῦ δ᾿ ἂν εἴη καὶ τῆς αὐτῆς δυνάμεως καὶ σοφίας καὶ τὸ διατεθρυμμένον πλήθει ζώων παντοδαπῶν, ὁπόσα τοῖς τοιούτοις σώμασιν ἐπιτρέχειν εἴωθε καὶ τὸν ἐκ τούτων ἀγείρειν κόρον, διακρῖναι μὲν ἐκεῖθεν, ἑνῶσαι δὲ πάλιν τοῖς οἰκείοις μέρεσι καὶ μορίοις, κἂν εἰς ἓν ἐξ ἐκείνων χωρήσῃ ζῶον, κἂν εἰς πολλά, κἂν ἐντεῦθεν εἰς ἕτερα, κἂν ἐκείνοις αὐτοῖς συνδιαλυθὲν ἐπὶ τὰς πρώτας ἀρχὰς ἐνεχθῇ κατὰ τὴν φυσικὴν εἰς ταύτας ἀνάλυσιν· ὃ δὴ καὶ μάλιστα ταράττειν ἔδοξέ τινας καὶ τῶν ἐπὶ σοφίᾳ θαυμαζομένων, ἰσχυρὰς οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὅπως ἡγησαμένων τὰς παρὰ τῶν πολλῶν φερομένας διαπορήσεις.
thought_title: God's power shown from creation itself
orientation: Athenagoras is arguing that God's power is sufficient for the resurrection, and he now points to the original creation of human bodies as proof.
pass_a_gloss: And indeed also the power, that it is sufficient for the resurrection of the bodies, the generation of these very things shows. For if he made the bodies of humans when they were not, according to the first constitution, and their principles, also when they have been dissolved, in whatever manner it may happen, he will raise them with equal ease; for to him this too is equally possible. And to the argument there is no harm, even if some suppose the first principles to be from matter, even if the bodies of humans to be from the elements as first things, even if from seeds. For of whatever power it is also to shape the matter considered by them to be formless, and to adorn the shapeless and unordered matter with many and different forms, and to gather the parts of the elements into one, and to divide the seed being one and simple into many, and to articulate the unarticulated, and to give life to the not living, of the same power it is also to unite the dissolved, and to raise the lying, and to make alive again the dead, and to change the corruptible into incorruptibility. And of the same would be also of the same power and wisdom also to separate from there the thing scattered among a multitude of all kinds of animals, as many as are accustomed to run upon such bodies and to gather their fill from these, and to unite again to the proper parts and members, even if it goes into one animal from those, even if into many, even if from there into others, even if dissolved together with those very animals it is brought to the first principles according to the natural dissolution into these; which very thing seemed especially to trouble some even of those admired for wisdom, who considered, I do not know how, strong the perplexities brought forward by the many.

lemmas.gloss: to scatter, to break in pieces

choices.why: The glossary requires 'resurrection' for ἀνάστασις, and the genitive plural σωμάτων is rendered as 'of the bodies' to keep the literal force.
σύστασις refers to the original formation or constitution of human bodies; 'constitution' preserves the sense of a structured putting-together.
εὐμάρεια means ease or facility; 'with equal ease' captures the comparative force of ἴσης.

choices.english: to change the corruptible into incorruptibility
choices.why: The glossary requires 'incorruptibility' for ἀφθαρσία (here in the form ἀρθαρσίαν, a variant spelling); 'corruptible' for φθαρτόν keeps the contrast.
rejected: to transform the perishable into imperishability
to change the corruptible into immortality

choices.why: διαθρύπτω means to break in pieces or scatter; the perfect participle passive is rendered as 'the thing scattered' to keep the passive force.

choices.term: τὰς παρὰ τῶν πολλῶν φερομένας διαπορήσεις
choices.english: the perplexities brought forward by the many
choices.why: διαπόρησις means perplexity or difficulty; 'brought forward' renders φερομένας in its passive sense of being adduced or advanced.
rejected: the difficulties carried by the many
the puzzles brought by the multitude

pass_b_english: Moreover, the very origin of these bodies shows that God's power is sufficient for the resurrection of the bodies. For if he made human bodies and their first principles when they did not exist at their original constitution, he will also raise them after they have been dissolved, in whatever manner it happens, with equal ease; for this too is equally possible for him. And the argument suffers no harm whether some suppose the first principles to be from matter, or human bodies to be from the elements as first things, or from seeds. For the power that is able to shape what they consider formless matter, to adorn what is shapeless and unordered with many different forms, to gather the parts of the elements into one, to divide the seed that is one and simple into many, to articulate what is unarticulated, and to give life to what is not living—that same power is able to unite what has been dissolved, to raise what lies fallen, to make alive again what has died, and to change the corruptible into incorruptibility. And it would belong to the same power and wisdom also to separate from there the thing scattered among a multitude of all kinds of animals—as many as are accustomed to attack such bodies and gather their fill from them—and to unite it again to its proper parts and members, whether it has passed from those animals into one animal or into many, or from there into others, or whether, dissolved together with those very animals, it has been carried back to the first principles according to the natural dissolution into them. This is what seemed especially to trouble some, even among those admired for wisdom, who somehow considered strong the perplexities brought forward by the many.

last_rejected.quote: to shape what they consider formless matter
last_rejected.source_quote: τὴν παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς νενομισμένην ἄμορφον οὖσαν μορφῶσαι
last_rejected.why: παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς means 'by them' (i.e., by the philosophers mentioned), 'in their opinion.' 'What they consider' captures this. But ἄμορφον οὖσαν is 'being formless'—the English adds 'matter' which is not in the Greek. The Greek says 'what they consider being formless' not 'formless matter.' This is an addition.
last_rejected.fix: to shape what they consider to be without form
last_rejected.ruling: ἄμορφον οὖσαν modifies νενομισμένην; 'matter' is contextually implied by ὕλης earlier. Addition is interpretive, not meaning-changing.

last_rejected.quote: to gather the parts of the elements into one
last_rejected.source_quote: τὰ μέρη τῶν στοιχείων εἰς ἓν συναγαγεῖν
last_rejected.why: τὰ μέρη τῶν στοιχείων is 'the parts of the elements'—but this likely means 'the parts [derived] from the elements' or 'elemental parts.' The English is literal but potentially misleading: it sounds like the elements themselves have parts, rather than parts made from elements. However, this is within normal range. No error.
last_rejected.ruling: τὰ μέρη τῶν στοιχείων literally 'parts of the elements'; within normal range. Not misleading.

last_rejected.quote: This is what seemed especially to trouble some, even among those admired for wisdom, who somehow considered strong the perplexities brought forward by the many.
last_rejected.source_quote: ὃ δὴ καὶ μάλιστα ταράττειν ἔδοξέ τινας καὶ τῶν ἐπὶ σοφίᾳ θαυμαζομένων, ἰσχυρὰς οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὅπως ἡγησαμένων τὰς παρὰ τῶν πολλῶν φερομένας διαπορήσεις.
last_rejected.why: The English loses the switch to the Critics' voice. The source marks this as objectors' words (per voices brief: 'which especially seemed to trouble some'). The English presents it as Athenagoras' own narration without marking the critics' perspective. The 'some' are the critics, but the English 'who somehow considered strong the perplexities' makes it sound like Athenagoras describing them, not their own objection being introduced. Actually the voice marking is subtle in Greek too. But the brief says this section is Critics (objectors). The English does not clearly signal this voice shift.
last_rejected.fix: This, they say, is what especially troubled them—some even admired for wisdom—who somehow thought the difficulties raised by the many were strong ones.
last_rejected.ruling: Greek ἔδοξέ τινας is indirect narration, not direct speech; no voice shift is marked in source itself.

last_rejected.why: τὸ κείμενον is 'what lies' (i.e., dead body), 'the fallen.' 'What lies fallen' is slightly redundant but captures meaning. No error.
last_rejected.ruling: τὸ κείμενον = 'what lies'; 'fallen' is within normal range for context. No error.
